slide.title: Choose Fairly, Test Once
slide.body: Four bars with range marks (baseline, frozen, fine-tuned, fine-tuned + schedule); two overlap and the simpler one is circled. A sealed envelope labelled TEST. Small tag: Deep Learning and Neural Networks · Lesson 19 · Capstone step 2.

scenes.voiceover: You have a baseline and a plan. This week, you train several models, and one will look best. The hard part is not training them. It is saying honestly that the winner really is better, and then testing it exactly once.

slide.title: Run the plan in order
slide.body: Baseline → pretrained model (ResNet, L10, or small encoder, L13) → + regularisation (L09) → + tuning (L16). One change per step.

scenes.voiceover: Run your plan in order. Start with the experiment most likely to give a large gain, usually a pretrained model. A ResNet for images, or a small encoder from the Hub for text. Then add regularisation and tuning, one change at a time.

slide.title: After every run
slide.body: Log a row to the results table (L17) · mark the hypothesis: supported, not supported, unclear · record the checkpoint name and licence

scenes.voiceover: After each run, log a row to your results table, and write one line in your plan. Was the hypothesis supported? Keep failed runs too. They are evidence for your report. Also record the name and licence of every pretrained checkpoint you use.

slide.title: A fair comparison
slide.body: Same validation split and preprocessing · same main metric · comparable budget, or a note · extra seeds for the leaders (L14)

scenes.voiceover: Compare fairly. Every run must use the same validation split and preprocessing, and the same main metric, computed the same way. Budgets must be comparable, or noted. And the leading candidates need more than one seed.

slide.title: Choose, then test once
slide.body: Validation results → written choice + reason (within seed variation? pick the simpler) → one arrow to a sealed TEST envelope, opened once → report the number.

scenes.voiceover: Choose the final model on validation data, and justify it. The best score is not the only reason. If two models are within seed variation, prefer the smaller, faster or simpler one. Then, and only then, evaluate it once on the test split. If you change the model after seeing the test result, the test score is no longer honest, and you must say so.

scenes.on_screen_text: Same dish, same judges, one tasting
scenes.voiceover: It is like judging a cooking competition. Every chef cooks the same dish, with the same ingredients and time, for the same judges. The final public tasting happens once. If a chef could taste the judges' plate and then cook again, it would not be fair.

Diego is an engineer at an avocado exporter in Uruapan, Mexico. His capstone classifies leaf photos into four classes, from a public dataset with a confirmed licence. His baseline is a small CNN trained from scratch.

screen_steps: Show the four runs: baseline CNN, frozen ResNet-18, resnet18_ft_layer4, fine-tuned + schedule
scenes.voiceover: In Colab, he loads his results table from Drive, so nothing is lost when a session ends. It has four runs. The baseline CNN, a frozen ResNet eighteen with a new head, the same with its last block fine-tuned, and the fine-tuned model with a learning-rate schedule.

screen_steps: Run the top two settings with 2 more seeds each; new rows appear in results.csv
scenes.on_screen_text: Mean, spread and count per run
scenes.voiceover: He reruns the top two with two more seeds. Then he groups the table by run, and shows the mean, the spread and the count of validation F1, sorted from best to worst. Two extra seeds per run is a small cost for an honest comparison.

screen_steps: Highlight the two fine-tuned rows and their overlapping ranges
Add a text cell: Final choice: resnet18_ft_layer4 (no schedule). Reason: within seed variation of the scheduled run, and simpler.
scenes.voiceover: The two fine-tuned runs are within seed variation of each other. So Diego chooses the version without the schedule, because it is simpler and equally good. He writes that reason next to the table, before he touches the test set.

screen_steps: Run once: final = load_checkpoint("resnet18_ft_layer4"); test_f1 = evaluate(final, test_dl); print("TEST macro F1:", round(test_f1, 3))
Copy the printed test score into the report draft
scenes.voiceover: Now he reloads the chosen checkpoint, and evaluates it on the test set, exactly once. He copies the number into his report, and does not change the model afterwards. If he changed it now, the test score would no longer be an honest estimate.

scenes.on_screen_text: Never pick the best test score
scenes.voiceover: A common mistake is evaluating every candidate on the test set, just to see, and then picking the best test score. This makes the test set a second validation set, and the reported score is too optimistic. Another is comparing runs with different validation splits, for example because the split was made without a fixed seed. Check the split is identical across all runs.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. One change at a time, pretrained first, log every run. 2. Same split and metric, extra seeds, prefer simpler. 3. Test once; report without changes.

scenes.voiceover: Let's recap. First, run planned experiments one change at a time, starting with a pretrained model, and log every run with its config. Second, compare on the same validation split and metric, use extra seeds for the leaders, and prefer the simpler model when results are within seed variation. Third, evaluate the chosen model once on the test set, and report that number without further changes.

Now it is your turn. This is capstone step two. In the exercise below this video, you will run at least three tracked experiments, choose your final model, and evaluate it once on the test set. Check your work against the capstone rubric. It takes about ninety minutes. In the final lesson, capstone step three, you document your experiments. See you there.
